summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys the Jewish people: their Middle Eastern genetic origins and shared ancestry, population size and distribution across Israel, the United States, Europe and the Americas, and the difficulty of counting them given differing definitions of who is a Jew. It also covers Ashkenazi and Sephardi divisions, centuries of antisemitic persecution, the mid-20th-century exodus of Jews from Arab and Muslim countries, and the role of religion and culture in Jewish identity.
one_line: Overview of the Jewish people covering origins, genetics, global population figures, definitions of Jewish identity, persecution, and migration history.
key_facts: Genetic studies show most Jews worldwide bear a common genetic heritage originating in the Middle East, most resembling peoples of the Fertile Crescent.
Jewish groups share a common genetic pool dating back 4,000 years, according to the note.
The Fiscus Judaicus, a tax imposed on Jews in 70 CE, was relaxed to exclude Christians in 96 CE.
A report published in 2014 stated about 43% of all Jews reside in Israel (6.1 million) and 40% in the United States (5.7 million).
Ashkenazi Jews represent at least 70% of Jews worldwide, and up to 90% prior to World War II and the Holocaust.
A 2008 study in the American Journal of Human Genetics found 19.8% of the modern Iberian population has Sephardic Jewish ancestry.
The Spanish Inquisition was led by Tomás de Torquemada, and the note cites the First Crusade as resulting in the massacre of Jews.
Traditionally, Jews are said to descend mostly from the Israelite tribes of Judah and Benjamin, and partially from the tribe of Levi.
Currently, the largest Jewish community outside Israel is in the United States, with 5.2 million to 6.4 million Jews by various estimates.
Currently, Jews account for 75.4% of the Israeli population, or 6 million people.
Between 1948 and 1958, the Jewish population of Israel rose from 800,000 to two million.
Prior to 1948, approximately 800,000 Jews lived in lands now making up the Arab world, excluding Israel.
Today around 26,000 Jews live in Arab countries and around 30,000 in Iran and Turkey.
France has between 483,000 and 500,000 Jews, the largest Jewish community in Western Europe and the third-largest in the world.
The United Kingdom has a Jewish community of 292,000, and Germany's 102,000 registered Jews form a slowly declining population.
